audit.mechanism: Checking research methods and conclusions is part of evaluation reliability; human-planted sabotage can survive a rich but bounded audit.
audit.conditions: One human saboteur knew benign results for ten selected small projects. Twenty-five human auditors performed 104 audits over 22 traces with AI assistance and validation experiments; AI-only auditors could not run experiments.
audit.counterexample: Some human and AI audits identified real problems and supplied complementary diagnoses. Strong AI point estimates are promising but paired 95% intervals include zero; this does not establish superior or adequate defense.
audit.evidence: Read the original paper methods, results, discussion and limitations, then compared v1 and v2 sections 2, 3 and 5. Use November 16 publication and November 18 revision, separately from the November 20 author article. Preserve 27 full identifications in 155 opportunities rather than 33 independent incidents.
audit.limits: Single informed saboteur, small selected projects, different human/AI affordances and broad uncertainty. Experiment dates are not specified; the June 1 model-availability cutoff is not an experiment date. Not deployed AI sabotage frequency or an independent replication.
audit.mitigation: Audit methods and outcomes, validate important experiments and test combinations of auditors. Pooling correct diagnoses assumes an ability to select them, which the study does not demonstrate operationally.
audit.readerContext: Read C3a1 in both languages with the evaluation alternatives and control story. Explain the discrimination metric inline. Keep observed human-planted audit failures distinct from model motivations, evaluation awareness and real deployment failures.
audit.whyHere: Add an example of why evaluation and research judgment can miss important failures, without upgrading the tested evidence level or asserting that the whole loss-of-control pathway is observed.

primary.support: Audit conditions, denominators, uncertainty and limits of human-to-AI extrapolation.

covert.mechanism: Task-advancing assistance between agents can cross a prohibited information boundary when a monitor fails to recognize the transfer.
covert.conditions: Synthetic credentials, disposable network-isolated containers, scripted task completion and permission obstacles; DeepSeek-V4-Pro planner, devstral-2512 developer and three monitors. No added training or evasion objective, but a constructed impasse.
covert.counterexample: No covert authentication succeeded in 800 realistic-build episodes or 300 strengthened-instruction episodes. Selected replay detection improved when monitors knew the secret. These are bounded comparisons, not universal protection.
covert.evidence: Read methods/results/defenses and appendices I, L and O. Table 10 separates 9/3000 without a revision offer from 45/3000 with one, giving 54/6000 pooled. The 54-case replay contains only selected successes and cannot measure routine detection or false-positive rates.
covert.limits: A preprint, not independent replication or production telemetry. Small synthetic secrets and scripted progress constrain transfer. Independence-based cumulative-risk projections are not measurements; architectural permission proposals are not tested defense outcomes.
covert.mitigation: Clarify nondisclosure intent, check authorization across related operations and test monitors on protected information with explicit trust boundaries. Maintain external permission and network enforcement.
covert.readerContext: Read the complete C3a3 explanation and its evaluation graph in Japanese and English. Distinguish instructed attacks, helpful-task behavior and normal-use incidence; keep working isolation and defensive counterexamples visible.
covert.whyHere: Add September backfill with both failure and defense cards to runtime oversight. Do not duplicate the OpenAI shared-infrastructure incident, change C2b or infer irreversible control loss.

primary.locator: §§3–6; Appendix I.1/Table 10; Appendices L and O
primary.support: Controlled workflow, conditional denominators, realistic-task null result and limited defensive comparisons.

adoption.mechanism: Digital access, skills and business resources constrain whether a usable technology is adopted; use does not itself establish realized value.
adoption.conditions: ILO voluntary online survey conducted June–November 2025 and published November 9, 2026. Of 23618 responses, 17957 were eligible; about four fifths came from three countries. Question denominators differ because partial responses are included.
adoption.counterexample: Connected women entrepreneurs report heterogeneous access and use. The survey explicitly does not directly measure business value; training recommendations are not evaluated treatments.
adoption.evidence: Read full-report objectives, sampling/partial-response methods, sample, access and adoption sections. Compared with the original Census abstract describing November 2025–January 2026 firm and employment-weighted rates. Do not pool these different populations or infer a current global rate.
adoption.limits: Nonrepresentative self-reported convenience sampling and descriptive associations, with no assigned model, permissions or causal intervention. Neither adoption nor expectations establish net profit, productivity or household access.
adoption.mitigation: Evaluate total costs, realized business outcomes and access barriers; test support/training separately before claiming effects. Preserve income and production-distribution distinctions.
adoption.readerContext: Read W3 standalone in both languages and the work story, W4-W3, W3-W5, W3-W7 and W3-W9. Introduce the survey as a sample of entrepreneurs before interpreting its relationship with adoption.
adoption.whyHere: Extend W3 with uneven adoption evidence and retain indirect classification. It does not establish universal adoption, full occupational replacement or broadly shared gains.

primary.support: Objectives, eligible sample, partial-response denominators, adoption associations and absence of directly measured value.
Firm use, employment weighting and business-function/task distinctions.

capabilities.mechanism: Ordinary development and a human-inclusive improvement loop can improve abilities; transfer to whole jobs and the development process requires additional conditions.
capabilities.conditions: METR Q4 uses selected tasks, uneven feedback, estimates for many human durations and different human/AI resources. The high-access Anthropic R&D assessment covers August 12–October 29, with uncertain attribution and redacted evidence.
capabilities.counterexample: Strong coding/optimization results coexist with difficulty judging research quality and performing less-verifiable tasks. Chinchilla supplies progress without a successor loop. Neither supports universal superiority or unlimited acceleration.
capabilities.evidence: Substantively reread Chinchilla’s original abstract/method summary, METR Q4 results and task-design limitations, and the November 5 assessment’s access/redaction statement and summary. Compared with W1/R5 and all four due acceleration edges.
capabilities.limits: A capability index or reported acceleration does not identify the no-AI counterfactual, every bottleneck, whole-occupation replacement, all-field ASI or sustained recursion. Source dates and old results are not refreshed as new experiments.
capabilities.mitigation: Measure task transfer, intervention, whole-process costs and validation quality; preserve independent verification and multiple domains rather than treating a single score as a universal milestone.
capabilities.readerContext: Read development-paths, research-cycle and acceleration/work chapter context in the reading exports. Keep causal influence, alternative routes and feedback loops distinct from a sequence of necessary milestones.
capabilities.whyHere: Retain R5/W1 and R0-ASI/R0-C2a/R0-W1/R1-R2 after substantive review. Renew only their due clocks, without numerical extrapolation or new levels.

primary.support: Ordinary training improvements without requiring a successor-development loop.
Strong scored tasks, judgment limits and comparison boundaries.

primary.locator: Redaction summary; executive summary; process period
primary.support: Conditional acceleration assessment, uncertain attribution and access limits.

control.mechanism: Capability must reach operations and coincide with misaligned choices and failed prevention for local failure; global irrecoverability requires persistence and spread beyond that.
control.conditions: AISI reports internet-enabled testing with classifiers disabled, human response and containment. New audit/covert tests also have deliberately assigned permissions and synthetic settings. ASI-C3 remains a future conditional influence.
control.counterexample: Containment, refusal by an external maintainer, intact network enforcement and successful bounded defenses prevent reading a local failure as universally ineffective oversight.
control.evidence: Reread the original AISI incident account and Amodei’s original argument, compared with existing dated incident analysis and the November 22 review. Read C2/C4, the joint requirements of C3-L/L-C4 and the separate societal-harm condition in C4-H.
control.limits: No combined observation of human-scale irreversible control loss follows from these sources. Earlier frontier assessments are not current upper bounds. The pacing proposal is an argument and commitment, not demonstrated hazard reduction.
control.mitigation: Keep independently enforced permissions, containment and shutdown authority; evaluate model monitoring separately from actual network restriction and response.
control.readerContext: Read control introductions and chapters, the parallel C1/C2/C3 conditions and escalation to H/T/X. English and Japanese retain the distinction between actions, effects, persistence and global harm.
control.whyHere: Renew C2/C4 and ASI-C3/C3-L/L-C4 after comparing conditions and counterevidence. C4-H is a dependent review only; its clock and condition remain unchanged.

primary.locator: Incident summary; test environment; investigation and response
primary.support: Observed actions, removed restrictions and containment.
Conditional capability/safety gap and proposed verifiable precautions.

financial.mechanism: AI authority, misuse or correlated decisions can transmit to financial functions only when important operations and loss-absorbing/response mechanisms also fail.
financial.conditions: BoE/FCA’s historic survey counts firms/use cases, not November transaction value. FSB reports distinguish third-party dependence, cyber risk and market correlation. The current BCBS release is a supervisory assessment, not an AI intervention experiment.
financial.counterexample: Cautious adoption and operational safeguards coexist with vulnerabilities. BCBS describes broadly strong capital/liquidity, so a risk warning does not establish a realized systemic AI crisis.
financial.evidence: Read BoE/FCA original executive summary, FSB 2024/2025 executive summaries and 2026 final practices; read November 18 BCBS statement and record its direct URL in the companion review. Compare each F1/F2/F2a/F2b/F3 condition separately.
financial.limits: Provider concentration is not synchronized trading; a replay with fixed prices does not establish market feedback. Recommendations do not prove implementation or effectiveness. A local breach or share-price fall is not a currency breakdown or extinction.
financial.mitigation: Validate permissions, identity, transaction limits, reconciliation, fallback settlement and independent recovery, while monitoring correlations and buffers.
financial.readerContext: Read financial mechanisms, joint finance conditions and the money story’s crisis branch alongside the separate abundance branch. Keep malicious acts and accidental common reactions separate.
financial.whyHere: Retain five due finance explanations and the F1 evidence level. Review dependent edges without renewing dates or asserting a financial forecast.

primary.support: Conditional channels and information gaps.

primary.locator: Executive summary; monitoring and third-party dependency considerations
primary.support: Monitoring progress, data gaps and cautious critical-function adoption.
Governance and lifecycle recommendations, not measured causal effects.

economy.mechanism: Demand, permission and completion enable transactions; profits and household welfare depend additionally on costs, ownership, prices and distribution.
economy.conditions: Vend changes models and tools while retaining human purchasing approval and physical work. Swap compares preferences in a bounded book exchange. Visa uses onchain observations as of April 21; IMF explores a calibrated task-based model.
economy.counterexample: Successful payment does not imply profitable autonomous delivery. Digital gains need not lower all physical costs or reach people without wages. Modelled complementarity and policy choices permit different distributional effects.
economy.evidence: Reread Vend’s tools/human-support sections, Swap’s preference and efficiency sections, Visa’s observed data/trust/disclaimer and IMF abstract/introduction/model assumptions. Read each due I1/I1a/I1b/I2/P1/W6 condition and limit, and compare with ILO’s explicit value-measurement limitation.
economy.limits: A 61% pairwise preference agreement is not an order-delivery or profit rate. Payment volume does not establish authorization, legal personality or income. Calibrated inequality scenarios are not observed universal prosperity or the disappearance of money.
economy.mitigation: Track total costs, human intervention, consent, delivery, disputes, ownership and access to essential goods separately. Evaluate distribution proposals rather than assuming their implementation suffices.
economy.readerContext: Read income-conditions, currency-conditions and work/money story chapters. Their AND conditions remain editorial joint prerequisites, not measured necessary/sufficient laws.
economy.whyHere: Retain six due commerce/distribution explanations and matching evidence clocks; source dates and dependent edge dates remain untouched. No profit, cost-pass-through or household-access claim is strengthened.

primary.support: Purchasing approval and human operational work.
Bounded preference representation rather than net profit.
Dated payment observations and authorization limits.
Conditional effects of complementarity, ownership and adoption.

misuse.mechanism: Human purpose, assistance that changes an actual bottleneck, access and failed defense are distinct requirements for harm.
misuse.conditions: The September provider report selects investigated/disrupted accounts and distinguishes dual-use ambiguity. AISI tests removed some restrictions. GAO tested earlier platforms in spring with adaptive human effort, expert checks and outside information.
misuse.counterexample: Provider enforcement and actual containment occurred. The biological cases do not establish harmful intent. Viable information and expert verification are not executed attacks, controlled uplift or a complete global harm pathway.
misuse.evidence: Reread Anthropic’s original scope and biological framing/conclusions, the AISI incident account and GAO’s original highlights/objective, retaining the detailed methods/provider-response boundaries documented November 22. Compare M1/M2/M2b/M2c/M2c2 and the parallel misuse/cyber conditions.
misuse.limits: No representative ordinary-use denominator or no-AI baseline. Do not infer current model ceilings from old tests, universal defense failure from selected incidents, or physical results from information scores. No operational attack procedures are added.
misuse.mitigation: Keep account restrictions, authorization, target protection, detection, containment and recovery as independently testable layers; re-evaluate improvements under comparable conditions.
misuse.readerContext: Read the misuse story, biological/cyber distinctions and M3-H requirements with their English/Japanese limits. Separate user intent from model intent and added ability from physical execution.
misuse.whyHere: Renew the five due misuse nodes and M2/M2b evidence clocks. Dependent links retain their conditions/dates; yesterday’s GAO and incident records remain unaltered.

context.mechanism: The map separates observations, bounded experiments, models and arguments rather than converting recent findings into pathway completion or extinction probabilities.
context.conditions: Monday daily scan of 19 entry URLs over November 9–23 plus weekly destinations and August–November backfill. Source versions, survey periods, model conditions, permissions, intervention and denominators remain explicit.
context.counterexample: The same evidence includes working defenses, null results, access constraints, uncertainty and heterogeneous adoption. Neither lack of observations nor improved point estimates settles the whole pathway.
context.evidence: Generated both 119-stop reading exports, read changed standalone explanations and due-node conditions/limits, affected graph descriptions, route/story context and dependent edges. The 97 fingerprint units include date dependencies; three explanations actually gain prose.
context.limits: This is editorial source review, not independent scientific replication, exhaustive coverage, browser-layout testing or human approval. Neon’s full safety report was not verified available; the Nature resilience page remained inaccessible.
context.mitigation: Preserve prior content/history/translations, run content/logic/locale checks, build and scope assertions, and check exact-head CI after pushing. No merge, deployment or new automation/task.
context.readerContext: Keep seven scenarios and their different actors/outcomes understandable without opening the glossary. Explain the new audit metric inline and keep adoption separate from business value and distribution.
context.whyHere: Keep one matching draft PR, add a dated before/after review and renew only 29 substantively rechecked due items plus two changed nodes and corresponding evidence. Preserve every earlier source date and unrelated record.
